en: Itivuttaka 51: Tikanipāta, Paṭhamavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having been said by the Sublime One, it was so heard by me: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a young jasmine flower (*sumana*), the person who is like a blue lotus (*utpala*), and the person who is like a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*). And how, monks, is one a person like a young jasmine flower? Here, monks, a certain person is of good birth, of noble lineage, and of pure descent, tracing back seven generations on both his maternal and paternal sides, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth. He is handsome, pleasing, and beautiful, possessing supreme beauty of complexion. He is wealthy, with great riches and abundant possessions, with vast wealth and grain, with a full treasury and granary.

He is virtuous, endowed with virtue, restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in even the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the training precepts. Just as a young jasmine flower is of good color, sweet fragrance, and exquisite scent; even so, monks, this person is of good birth... [as above] ...and sees fear in even the slightest faults, training himself by undertaking the training precepts. This, monks, is called a person like a young jasmine flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is of good birth... [as above] ...and sees fear in even the slightest faults, training himself by undertaking the training precepts. He is learned, one who has heard much, a bearer of what he has heard, a storehouse of what he has heard; those teachings which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, remembered, recited verbally, investigated with the mind, and penetrated well through view. Just as a blue lotus, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water; even so, monks, this person is of good birth... [as above] ...and has penetrated well through view. This, monks, is called a person like a blue lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a white lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is of good birth... [as above] ...and has penetrated well through view. He is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the spiritual life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. Just as a white lotus, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands completely unsoiled by the water; even so, monks, this person is of good birth... [as above] ...and is liberated through final knowledge. This, monks, is called a person like a white lotus. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Happy One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, friends! “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “In that the Blessed One spoke in brief thus: ‘Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world,’ it would be good, friends, if the Venerable Ones would each explain the detailed meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One. Perhaps we might hear from the Venerable Ones the detailed meaning of this statement as spoken in brief by the Blessed One. “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred, saying: “It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain the detailed meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One. “Ānanda, the person like a young jasmine flower is inferior, the person like a blue lotus is middling, and the person like a white lotus is superior. And how, Ānanda, is one a person like a young jasmine flower? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is of good birth... [as above] ...and sees fear in even the slightest faults, training himself by undertaking the training precepts. This, Ānanda, is called a person like a young jasmine flower. And how, Ānanda, is one a person like a blue lotus? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is of good birth... [as above] ...and has penetrated well through view. This, Ānanda, is called a person like a blue lotus. And how, Ānanda, is one a person like a white lotus? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is of good birth... [as above] ...and is liberated through final knowledge. This, Ānanda, is called a person like a white lotus. These, Ānanda, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Happy One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. The Discourse on Elements.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard:
"Bhikkhus, there are these three elements."
“What three?
The element of form, the element of the formless, and the element of cessation—
these, monks, are the three elements.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
With regard to this, it is said:
“Having fully understood the realm of form...”
Not settled in the formless realms,
those people who are liberated in cessation are the ones who have abandoned death.
Having touched with the body the deathless element,
which is free from acquisitions,
[he realizes] the relinquishing of all acquisitions.
Having realized it for himself, the Tathāgata, free from taints,
the Perfectly Enlightened One,
teaches the sorrowless, dust-free state.
This matter too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The second [sutta].
